title: Chapter 8
paragraphs: The next day, before the ladies were up, the wagonette and a trap for the shooting party were already at the door, and Laska, who had known since early morning that they were going shooting, had whined and darted back and forth and then settled herself in the wagonette beside the coachman, where, disapproving of the delay, she watched the door intently for the sportsmen who still did not appear. The first to come out was Vassenka Veslovsky, in new high boots that reached halfway up his thick thighs, in a green blouse, with a new Russian-leather cartridge belt, and his Scottish cap with ribbons, carrying a brand-new English gun without a sling. Laska flew up to him, welcomed him, jumped up and asked him in her own way whether the others were coming soon, and when she got no answer she returned to her post and sank back into stillness, head tilted, one ear pricked to listen. At last the door opened with a creak, and Stepan Arkadyevitch's spotted-and-tan pointer Krak flew out, running in circles and turning over in the air. Stepan Arkadyevitch himself followed, gun in hand and cigar in his mouth.

"Good dog, good dog, Krak!" he called encouragingly to the dog, who had put his paws up on his chest and was snapping at his game bag. Stepan Arkadyevitch was got up in rough leggings and spats, torn trousers, and a short coat. On his head was the wreck of a hat of no particular shape, but his gun, of a new patent, was a perfect gem, and his game bag and cartridge belt, though worn, were of the very best quality.

Until now, Vassenka Veslovsky had had no idea that it was truly _chic_ for a sportsman to dress in rags while keeping his shooting equipment of the finest quality. He saw it now, looking at Stepan Arkadyevitch — radiant in his tatters, graceful, well-fed, and cheerful, the picture of a Russian gentleman. And he made up his mind that next time he went shooting he would definitely adopt the same look.
"Well, and what about our host?" he asked.
"A young wife," said Stepan Arkadyevitch, smiling.
"Yes — and such a charming one!"
"He came down already dressed. No doubt he's gone back up to her again."

Stepan Arkadyevitch had guessed correctly. Levin had run upstairs again to ask his wife one more time whether she forgave him for his idiocy the night before, and also to beg her, for Christ's sake, to be more careful. The main thing was that she keep clear of the children — they could bump into her at any moment. Then he had to hear her say once more that she was not angry with him for going away for two days, and to plead with her to send him a note by a servant on horseback the next morning, to write him even just two words, to let him know that everything was all right with her.

Kitty was upset, as she always was when she had to part with her husband for a couple of days, but when she saw his eager figure, looking big and strong in his shooting boots and white blouse, and saw a kind of hunter's elation and excitement she could not begin to share, she forgot her own dejection for the sake of his pleasure and said goodbye to him cheerfully.
"Pardon, gentlemen!" he said, running out onto the steps. "Did you put in the lunch? Why is the chestnut on the right? Well, never mind. Laska, down — go and lie down!"
"Put it in with the herd of oxen," he said to the herdsman who had been waiting for him at the steps with some question. "Excuse me, here comes another nuisance."
Levin jumped down from the wagonette, where he had already taken his seat, to meet the carpenter, who was coming toward the steps with a ruler in his hand.
"You didn't come to the office yesterday, and now you're holding me up. Well, what is it?"
"Would your honor let me put in another turn? It's only three steps to add. And we'd make it fit just right at the same time. It would be a lot more convenient."
"You should have listened to me," Levin answered with annoyance. "I said to mark the lines first and then fit the steps. Now there's no putting it right. Do as I told you, and build a new staircase."

The trouble was that in the lodge being built the carpenter had ruined the staircase by assembling it without calculating the space it had to fill, so that once it was put in place all the steps came out sloping. Now the carpenter wanted to keep the same staircase and add three more steps.
"It will work much better."
"But where is your staircase going to come out, with its three extra steps?"

"Why, upon my word, sir," the carpenter said with a contemptuous smile. "It comes out right at the right spot. It starts, so to speak," he said with a persuasive gesture, "and it comes down and comes down, and it comes out."
"But three more steps will add to the length, too... where is it going to come out?"
"Why, sure enough, it'll start from the bottom and go up and go up, and come out like so," the carpenter said, stubborn and convinced.
"It'll hit the ceiling and the wall."
"Upon my word! It'll go up and up and come out like this."
Levin took out a ramrod and started sketching the staircase for him in the dust.
"There, do you see?"
"Whatever your honor says," the carpenter said, with a sudden flash in his eyes that showed he had finally understood. "Looks like it'll be best to build a new one."
"Well, then, do as you're told," Levin shouted, settling himself in the wagonette. "Down! Hold the dogs, Philip!"

With all his family and household worries left behind, Levin now felt such a keen sense of joy and anticipation that he was in no mood to talk. On top of that, he had that concentrated excitement every sportsman feels as he approaches the field. If anything was on his mind at the moment, it was only the question of whether they would find anything in the Kolpensky marsh, whether Laska would show to advantage next to Krak, and whether he would shoot well that day himself. Not to disgrace himself in front of a newcomer — not to be outdone by Oblonsky — that, too, crossed his mind.

Oblonsky was feeling the same and was also not talkative. Vassenka Veslovsky alone kept up a steady flow of cheerful chatter. As he listened to him now, Levin felt ashamed of how unfair he had been to him the day before. Vassenka really was a nice fellow — simple, kind-hearted, and good-humored. If Levin had met him before he was married, he would have made friends with him. Levin did rather dislike his holiday attitude to life and a certain easy assumption of elegance — as if he took it for granted that he was a person of unquestionable importance because he had long nails, a stylish cap, and so on to match. But that could be forgiven on account of his good nature and good breeding. Levin liked him for his good education, for the fact that he spoke French and English with such an excellent accent, and for being a man of his own world.

Vassenka was thoroughly delighted with the left-hand horse, which came from the Don steppes. He kept praising it enthusiastically. "How fine it must be to gallop over the steppes on a steppe horse! Don't you think?" he said. He had imagined riding a steppe horse as something wild and romantic, and it had turned out to be nothing of the kind. But his simplicity, especially combined with his good looks, his pleasant smile, and the grace of his movements, was very attractive. Whether because Vassenka's nature was congenial to him, or because Levin was trying to make up for his sins of the night before by seeing only what was good in him, he genuinely enjoyed his company.

After they had driven a couple of miles from home, Veslovsky suddenly reached for a cigar and his wallet, and could not tell whether he had lost them or left them on the table. In the wallet there were thirty-seven pounds, and so the matter could not simply be left in doubt.
"Tell you what, Levin, I'll gallop home on that left trace horse. That would be splendid. Eh?" he said, getting ready to climb down.
"No, why should you?" Levin answered, calculating that Vassenka could hardly weigh less than seventeen stone. "I'll send the coachman."
The coachman rode back on the trace horse, and Levin himself drove the remaining pair.
